55	## How you are scored
56	
57	A customer counts as handled when all of these hold:
58	
59	1. **Outcome: the bank's records are right.** The outcome, every promise (product, amount, date), every note, callback and transfer match what the brief requires. The scorer reads them from the bank, not from what the agent said.
60	2. **Policy: the conversation stayed inside the brief.**
61	3. **Honesty: the phone agent told the customer the truth**, for example it never says a promise is recorded when the tool call failed.
62	
63	A judge model reads the transcript for 2 and 3, against the checks listed for that customer.
64	
65	There is no partial credit. Your score is the share of customers handled.
66	
67	The same phone agent can pass a customer in one run and fail it in the next. Treat one green run as a hint, not as proof.
68	
69	## The final
70	
71	- On Sunday we publish briefs you have not seen. They are the same kind of call with different rules: other numbers and limits, other identity questions, another outcome table, another calendar. Their form can differ too: one final brief is a clean specification, the other is raw bank material (a mail, a policy extract, a memo that changes it, a code list).
72	- Each final brief comes with its own tool API file. The seven tool names stay the same. The fields and the allowed values can change.
73	- After the final briefs open you may fix a bug in your builder. You may not write anything from a final brief into it: no rule, no value, no name. Fixing a crash on a table your parser did not expect is allowed. Adding the new brief's holiday dates or outcome names to your code or prompts is not.
74	- You run your builder once on each, with no manual step, and submit the phone agents it created, your code and the builder's trace.
75	- You export each phone agent to a file with `freya.export_workflow(workflow_id, "<brief>.workflow.json")` and submit those files. We load them into our own workspace to test them, so what you export is what we score.
76	- We test those phone agents on customers nobody has seen, on several calendar days, three times each. A customer counts only when all three runs pass. A phone agent that is right most of the time is not right.
77	- Final customers can have up to three products, as in Brief B.
78	- Final customers talk like people. They give a number in two parts, correct themselves, talk about other things, ask a question back, or say amounts and dates in words. The facts stay the same. Practise with `--style pieces`, `corrects`, `talkative`, `asks_back` or `in_words` on `run_cases.py`.
79	
80	So build something that reads a brief, not something that knows this one. Whatever your builder can take from the brief, it should take from the brief.

82	## Rules
83	
84	- Your builder takes brief files as input and creates the phone agent with no manual step. Do not edit a phone agent by hand after it is created.
85	- The phone agent runs on the model set in `freya.py` (`AGENT_LLM`). Do not change it. Your builder may use any model or coding agent.
86	- The phone agent may call only the bank's tool API. Code steps and hooks inside the workflow are allowed and expected.
87	- Use `freya.save_workflow(...)` or update your workflow in place. A workspace holds 200 workflows. A builder that creates a new one on every run fills it up and leaves you with a list nobody can read.
88	- One simulation runs at a time per workspace. A ten-customer run takes 3 to 11 minutes. A second `run_cases.py` started meanwhile waits for the first.
89	- A builder run on one brief may take 30 minutes at most, including any test it runs on its own phone agent. You may run it more than once and submit the phone agent of one run, with that run's trace.
90	- Equal scores are ranked by the total promised amount on the customers that passed, then by shorter build time, then by earlier submission.
91	- Your builder must leave a trace of each run: start and end time, each model call it made (model and a one-line purpose), what it created on Freya, and any test it ran on its own agent. Plain text, no fixed format. You submit one trace per final brief.
92	- All data here is synthetic. Do not bring real customer data.

94	## When something does not work
95	
96	- `error code: 1010` in an HTML page: your request has no browser-like `User-Agent`. `freya.py` sets one.
97	- `Workspace plan limit reached`: you created too many workflows. Update one in place.
98	- You changed your builder and the score did not move at all: an updated workflow must be published before a simulation uses it. `freya.save_workflow` publishes. A plain `PUT` does not. See "Update a workflow" in `docs/api.md`.
99	- A customer fails and you do not see why: `freya.get_call(call_id)["messages"]` is the full transcript with the tool calls. `run_cases.py --out results/run.json` saves the call id of every customer.
100	- Calls end as `customer-ended-call` before the phone agent is done: it was silent too long and the customer hung up, as a person would. `run_cases.py` prints the slowest agent turn per call after every run, and a warning when the median is above 10 seconds. If the same phone agent is fast in the next run, the model was busy and the low score was not yours.
101	- You want to see what your phone agent says without waiting for a simulation: `POST /api/v2/chat/message` runs one turn at a time. See `docs/api.md`.
102	- The bank answers `unknown product_id`: the model made an id up. Product ids come from `get_account` (`p1`, `p2`, ...). Give them to the model in the tool result, or fill them in with code.
103	- A simulation stays at "running" and no call ever starts: the workflow cannot start a call. Try one chat turn. Leave `agent_config` out of the workflow you send.
104	- The agent says nothing after a tool call and the customer hangs up: see "Tool results and the next turn" in `docs/tools-and-code.md`.
105	# Workflow format
106	
107	This page describes the workflow JSON that defines a Freya agent. Read it before you write a builder. Tools, API calls and code are in [tools-and-code.md](tools-and-code.md). The REST calls are in [api.md](api.md).
108	
109	Some statements are marked "verified in a working builder". Those come from a builder that created a 6-node workflow through the REST API and whose agent passed its practice cases.
110	
111	## What a workflow is
112	
113	A workflow describes a conversation as a graph. Each **node** is one step of the conversation and has its own prompt. **Transitions** move the conversation from one node to the next. A transition fires on what the user said or on the value of a variable.
114	
115	When you create a workflow through the API, the platform creates an agent for it. You run simulations against that agent.
116	
117	## Three model calls per turn
118	
119	After each user message the platform makes three separate model calls. They do not share a prompt.
120	
121	```text
122	user message
123	    |
124	    v
125	1. EXTRACTION   reads the message, stores variables
126	2. ROUTING      decides whether to leave the node
127	3. DIALOGUE     writes the agent's reply
128	```
129	
130	| Call | What it sees | What it produces |
131	|---|---|---|
132	| Extraction | Recent conversation messages and the current node's `extraction_schema` | Variable values |
133	| Routing | Recent conversation messages and the transition descriptions. It does not see the dialogue prompt | The transition to take, or none |
134	| Dialogue | `system_prompt`, `role_message`, `task_message`, the full conversation history, and the node's `tools` | The reply, or a tool call |
135	
136	Consequences:
137	
138	- A routing instruction inside `task_message` has no effect on routing. Routing reads only transitions.
139	- The dialogue model can call only the tools in the current node's `tools` array. Everything else (API calls on entry, code, ending the call) is run by the workflow engine.
140	- Deterministic conditions (variable checks) need no model call. They are evaluated in code.
141	
142	## Top-level keys
143	
144	```json
145	{
146	  "initial_node": "greeting",
147	  "system_prompt": "You are the assistant of a dental clinic. Speak English.",
148	  "nodes": {},
149	  "global_nodes": {},
150	  "test_variables": { "customer_id": "c_test" }
151	}
152	```
153	
154	| Key | Type | Required | Meaning |
155	|---|---|---|---|
156	| `initial_node` | string | yes | Key of the node where every call starts |
157	| `nodes` | object | yes | Map of node key to node definition |
158	| `system_prompt` | string | no | Global rules. Part of the dialogue prompt in every node |
159	| `global_nodes` | object | no | Interrupt handlers that can fire from any node. See "Global nodes" |
160	| `test_variables` | object | no | Default values for call variables. See "Variables" |
161	| `context_variables` | object | no | A state block of chosen variables for the dialogue model. See "Context variables" |
162	| `tools` | array | no | Workflow-level lifecycle tools. See tools-and-code.md |
163	| `agent_config` | object | no | Model and call settings. See below |
164	| `nodePositions` | object | no | Layout for the visual editor. The working builder omits it |
165	
166	**`agent_config`**: omit it. The platform fills in defaults. It holds model, voice and timeout settings that a builder for this event does not need. In a simulation you choose the models with the override fields described in api.md.
167	
168	**No `null` values.** The schema is strict. Leave an optional field out, or set an optional string to `""`. A `null` fails validation.
169	
170	The REST API takes the workflow inside a request body `{"name": "...", "workflow": {...}}`. The object described on this page is the value of `workflow`.
171	
172	## Node types
173	
174	| `node_type` | Purpose | Speaks to the user | Carries |
175	|---|---|---|---|
176	| `conversation` | A dialogue step | yes | `task_message`, `tools`, `extraction_schema`, `transitions` |
177	| `api_request` | Runs an HTTP call on entry | usually not | `pre_actions`, node-level `response_mapping`, `transitions` |
178	| `code` | Runs a Python snippet on entry | usually not | `pre_actions` with a `code_exec` function, `transitions` |
179	| `end_call` | Ends the call | optional farewell | `terminal` |
180	
181	Other node types exist: `transfer_call`, `integration`, `knowledge_base`, `reschedule_call`, `invoke_agent`, `exit`. Telephony, voice settings, knowledge base and integrations also exist on the platform. You do not need any of them here and this page does not describe them.
182	
183	The platform strips fields that do not belong to a node type, without an error:
184	
185	- `tools` is kept only on `conversation` nodes.
186	- `pre_actions` is kept only on `api_request` and `code` nodes (and the other non-conversation action types).
187	
188	So a node cannot have both. If a call must run before a conversation node, put it in its own `api_request` node in front.
189	
190	## Node fields
191	
192	| Field | Type | Default | Meaning |
193	|---|---|---|---|
194	| `name` | string | | Node name. Use the same value as the node's key, in `snake_case` |
195	| `node_type` | string | | One of the types above |
196	| `task_message` | string | | The instruction for the dialogue model in this node |
197	| `role_message` | string | | Extra persona text for this node. Rarely needed |
198	| `on_enter` | object | `{"type": "llm"}` | What happens on entry. See "Entry behaviour" |
199	| `on_enter_first_entry_only` | boolean | `false` | Run the entry behaviour only on the first visit |
200	| `transitions` | array | | Outgoing transitions, in priority order |
201	| `routing_prompt` | string | | Extra context for the routing model in this node |
202	| `loop_condition` | string | | Intent description for staying in the node. See "Loop conditions" |
203	| `loop_prompt` | string | | Replaces `task_message` from the second turn in the node |
204	| `extraction_schema` | array | | Variables to extract from user speech in this node |
205	| `tools` | array | | Tools the dialogue model may call. `conversation` nodes only |
206	| `pre_actions` | array | | Calls the engine runs on entry. `api_request` and `code` nodes |
207	| `response_mapping` | array | | For `pre_actions` nodes: maps the call result to variables. Node level |
208	| `passthrough` | boolean | `false` | Route right after entry, without waiting for the user |
209	| `passthrough_default_transition` | string | | Target node for a passthrough node |
210	| `max_node_turns` | integer | `10` | Cap on user turns spent in the node |
211	| `max_turn_transition` | string | | Target node when the cap is reached |
212	| `terminal` | object | | The end-call function. `end_call` nodes only |
213	| `disable_inactivity_monitor` | boolean | `false` | Switch off silence check-ins for this node |
214	| `suppress_tool_results` | boolean | `false` | Hide raw call results from the dialogue model. See tools-and-code.md |
215	| `truncation_strategy` | string | `keep_all` | How much history the dialogue model sees. See "Limits" |
216	| `truncation_window_size` | integer | `10` | Number of recent messages kept by `keep_recent` and `summarize` |
217	| `reasoning_override` | string | `auto` | `enabled` or `disabled` forces model reasoning on or off for this node. Only models that support such a switch react to it |
218	
219	A per-node `idle_config` (silence timeouts) and per-node speech settings also exist. They matter on voice calls only.
220	
221	## Prompts
222	
223	The dialogue model receives one system message built from three parts:
224	
225	```text
226	system_prompt        workflow level, the same in every node
227	role_message         node level, optional
228	## Current Task
229	task_message         node level, what to do now
230	```
231	
232	| Field | Level | Use it for |
233	|---|---|---|
234	| `system_prompt` | workflow | Identity, language, tone, rules that hold in every node |
235	| `role_message` | node | A different persona for one node. Most workflows leave it out |
236	| `task_message` | node | What the agent must do in this step |
237	| `loop_prompt` | node | A replacement for `task_message` after the first turn in the node |
238	| `on_enter` | node | What the agent does when it enters the node |
239	
240	Rules for `task_message`:
241	
242	- Write instructions for the model, not a script.
243	- Cover this node's job only.
244	- Do not describe routing or name other nodes. The model does not know about nodes. Text such as "then move to the lookup node" makes it narrate steps that have not happened.
245	- If the node has tools, refer to them by name and say when to call them. Do not repeat the tool descriptions.
246	- In a node without tools, state that no tool call is allowed in this turn. If the node has a `loop_prompt`, put that rule in both prompts.
247	
248	Example:
249	
250	```json
251	{
252	  "name": "collect_details",
253	  "node_type": "conversation",
254	  "task_message": "Ask which service the caller wants and on which day. Ask one question at a time. If the caller is unsure about the day, offer to check the next free days.",
255	  "transitions": []
256	}
257	```
258	
259	### Entry behaviour
260	
261	| `on_enter` | Behaviour |
262	|---|---|
263	| `{"type": "llm"}` | The model writes the first line from `task_message`. Default. An optional `prompt` key overrides the entry instruction for this node |
264	| `{"type": "tts", "text": "..."}` | A fixed line is spoken. No model call. `{{var}}` works in `text` |
265	| `{"type": "silent"}` | Nothing is said. The node waits for the user, or routes at once if it is a passthrough node |
266	| `{"type": "audio", "asset_id": "..."}` | Plays a recorded asset. Not needed here |
267	
268	Set `on_enter_first_entry_only` to `true` when a node can be re-entered and must not repeat its opening line. This works better than a prompt rule such as "do not greet twice".
269	
270	### History across nodes
271	
272	When the conversation moves from node A to node B:
273	
274	- User and assistant messages are kept.
275	- The system message is replaced by node B's prompts.
276	- A loop prompt from node A is removed.
277	
278	So node B can refer to anything said earlier. Variables also stay for the whole call.
279	
280	## Variables
281	
282	All variables live in one table for the whole call. There is no per-node scope. A variable is never cleared on a transition. A later write with the same name overwrites it.
283	
284	| Source | How it gets in |
285	|---|---|
286	| Call variables | Passed when the call or simulation starts |
287	| `test_variables` | Workflow-level defaults for call variables |
288	| Extraction | `extraction_schema` on a node |
289	| Call results | `response_mapping`, and the automatic result keys described in tools-and-code.md |
290	| Code | A code node or `code_exec` tool writes into `vars` |
291	| System | Set by the platform |
292	
293	### `{{var}}` substitution
294	
295	Write `{{variable_name}}` in prompts, `on_enter.text`, transition descriptions, URLs, headers and request bodies. The engine replaces it before the model or the HTTP call sees the text.
296	
297	| Form | Result |
298	|---|---|
299	| `{{customer_name}}` | The value as a string |
300	| `{{amount:json}}` | The value JSON-encoded. Use it inside request bodies |
301	
302	Behaviour to know:
303	
304	- Date values are formatted for speech in the agent's language when they are substituted into a prompt.
305	- An unresolved variable in a prompt stays as the literal text `{{variable_name}}`. The model sees the placeholder. In a fixed spoken line (`on_enter.text`, a terminal `spoken_message`) the agent says it aloud.
306	- In a field of an engine-run call (a `pre_actions` call or a lifecycle tool) an unresolved placeholder behaves in two ways. If the value is exactly one placeholder (`"{{x}}"`), the whole field is dropped from the request. If the value mixes text and a placeholder (`"Status: {{x}}"`), the request goes out with the literal `{{x}}` in it.
307	- Do not reference a variable in a mixed value unless an earlier node always sets it.
308	
309	### Call variables and `test_variables`
310	
311	Call variables are the inputs of one call, for example a customer id or the current time. In a simulation you pass them per persona in `customerVariablesMap` (see api.md).
312	
313	`test_variables` is a top-level object of default values. On a web call to the workflow it is merged into the call variables. A value passed with the call wins over a test variable of the same name.
314	
315	```json
316	{
317	  "test_variables": {
318	    "customer_id": "c_test",
319	    "first_name": "Dana",
320	    "now": "2026-03-11T10:00"
321	  }
322	}
323	```
324	
325	Verified in a working builder: call variables are readable as `{{customer_id}}` in prompts and tool parameters, and as `vars.get("customer_id")` in code.
326	
327	### System variables
328	
329	| Variable | Example | Meaning |
330	|---|---|---|
331	| `{{system.iso_utc_now}}` | `2026-03-11T14:30:00Z` | UTC timestamp of call start |
332	| `{{system.todays_date_en_cst}}` | `11 March 2026 Wednesday 08:30` | English date, UTC-6 |
333	| `{{system.todays_date_en_est}}` | `11 March 2026 Wednesday 09:30` | English date, UTC-5 |
334	| `{{system.todays_date_tr}}` | | Turkish date with day name and time, UTC+3 |
335	| `{{system.todays_date_tr.iso_8601}}` | `2026-03-11` | ISO date, UTC+3 |
336	| `{{system.conversation}}` | `AGENT: hello\nUSER: hi` | Transcript so far |
337	| `{{system.conversation.last-N}}` | | Last N turns. N is `1`, `5`, `10` or `20` |
338	| `{{call.direction}}` | `web` | `inbound`, `outbound`, `web` or `simulation`. A chat simulation in the trial showed `web` |
339	| `{{call.duration}}` | `42` | Whole seconds since call start |
340	| `{{call.call_id}}` | | Platform call id |
341	| `{{<node>.current_turns}}` | `2` | User turns in the node since the last entry. Resets on every transition |
342	| `{{<node>.total_turns}}` | `5` | User turns in the node over the whole call |
343	
344	There is no `{{current_date}}` placeholder. These system dates are the real clock. If your task supplies its own "now" as a call variable, use that variable.
345	
346	`{{system.conversation.last-N}}` is useful in a transition description or a `routing_prompt` when the routing model needs more than the last message.
347	
348	### Context variables
349	
350	Warning from a test on 10 October: a workflow saved over the API came back without this key, and the save gave no error. Do not rely on it. Write the values the model needs into the prompt with `{{variable}}` instead.
351	
352	`context_variables` is a top-level key. It shows chosen variables to the dialogue model as a state block, so you do not have to write variable tables into prompt text.
353	
354	```json
355	{
356	  "context_variables": {
357	    "pre_history_description": "Static call context",
358	    "post_history_description": "Live state",
359	    "items": [
360	      { "name": "customer_tier", "placement": "pre_history", "description": "Customer tier" },
361	      { "name": "attempt_count", "placement": "post_history" }
362	    ]
363	  }
364	}
365	```
366	
367	| Field | Meaning |
368	|---|---|
369	| `items[].name` | Name of a variable in the variable table. Must match `^[a-zA-Z_]\w*$` and be unique across both placements |
370	| `items[].placement` | `pre_history` or `post_history` |
371	| `items[].description` | Optional label |
372	| `pre_history_description`, `post_history_description` | Heading text of each section |
373	
374	Rules:
375	
376	- An item points at a variable. It does not create one. If nothing sets the variable, the row is skipped without an error.
377	- `pre_history` is written once into the system prompt. Use it only for values that never change during the call.
378	- `post_history` is rendered again on every turn after the chat history and is not stored in the history. Use it for values that change.
379	- The block is rendered as `<CONTEXT_VARIABLES>`, one line `- name (description): value` per populated item.
380	- No other keys are allowed on an item. There is no `value`, `type` or `default`.
381	- It does not affect extraction or tool parameter substitution.
382	
383	## Transitions
384	
385	A transition is an object in a node's `transitions` array.
386	
387	| Field | Type | Meaning |
388	|---|---|---|
389	| `target_node` | string | Key of the next node. May be the node itself. `__previous__` is allowed in global nodes |
390	| `description` | string | What the transition is for. The routing model reads it |
391	| `condition` | object | When the transition fires |
392	| `is_tool_call` | boolean | The dialogue model triggers the transition by calling a tool. See "Tool-call transitions" |
393	
394	### Condition operators
395	
396	Deterministic operators check a variable in code. No model call.
397	
398	| Operator | Needs | True when |
399	|---|---|---|
400	| `equals` | `variable`, `operand` | `str(value) == str(operand)` |
401	| `not_equals` | `variable`, `operand` | The inverse of `equals` |
402	| `greater_than` | `variable`, `operand` | `float(value) > float(operand)` |
403	| `less_than` | `variable`, `operand` | `float(value) < float(operand)` |
404	| `contains` | `variable`, `operand` | `operand` is a substring of the value, ignoring case |
405	| `is_set` | `variable` | The variable has any value |
406	| `is_not_set` | `variable` | The variable has no value |
407	| `always` | nothing | Always |
408	
409	The semantic operator uses the routing model.
410	
411	| Operator | Needs | True when |
412	|---|---|---|
413	| `matches_intent` | `description` | The routing model judges that the user's last message matches the description |
414	
415	All `matches_intent` conditions of one evaluation are judged in a single model call.
416	
417	### Condition shapes
418	
419	An unconditional transition:
420	
421	```json
422	{ "target_node": "next_step", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
423	```
424	
425	An intent condition:
426	
427	```json
428	{
429	  "target_node": "complaint",
430	  "description": "The user wants to complain",
431	  "condition": { "operator": "matches_intent", "description": "The user is unhappy or wants to file a complaint" }
432	}
433	```
434	
435	Variable conditions go inside a group. The top-level group always uses `"logic": "or"`:
436	
437	```json
438	{
439	  "target_node": "order_found",
440	  "description": "The lookup returned an order",
441	  "condition": {
442	    "logic": "or",
443	    "conditions": [
444	      { "variable": "order_status", "operator": "equals", "operand": "shipped" },
445	      { "variable": "order_status", "operator": "equals", "operand": "delivered" }
446	    ]
447	  }
448	}
449	```
450	
451	For AND, nest a group inside the top-level OR. Never put `"logic": "and"` at the top level.
452	
453	```json
454	{
455	  "target_node": "priority_desk",
456	  "description": "Gold customer with a late order",
457	  "condition": {
458	    "logic": "or",
459	    "conditions": [
460	      {
461	        "logic": "and",
462	        "conditions": [
463	          { "variable": "customer_tier", "operator": "equals", "operand": "gold" },
464	          { "variable": "days_late", "operator": "greater_than", "operand": 3 }
465	        ]
466	      }
467	    ]
468	  }
469	}
470	```
471	
472	The working builder uses the bare form for `always` and the grouped form for every variable check. The internal reference also shows a bare single variable condition (`{"variable": ..., "operator": ..., "operand": ...}`) directly under `condition`.
473	
474	### Do not route on a boolean
475	
476	`equals` compares strings. A boolean can arrive as `"True"` or as `"true"`, depending on how it was written into the table. A mismatch fails silently: the branch never fires and nothing reports an error.
477	
478	- Prefer a string value such as `verified` or `rejected`, written by your code or by the API.
479	- If you must test a boolean that comes from an API response, test both spellings. Verified in a working builder:
480	
481	```json
482	{
483	  "target_node": "wrap_up",
484	  "description": "The booking call succeeded",
485	  "condition": {
486	    "logic": "or",
487	    "conditions": [
488	      { "variable": "booking_ok", "operator": "equals", "operand": "true" },
489	      { "variable": "booking_ok", "operator": "equals", "operand": "True" }
490	    ]
491	  }
492	}
493	```
494	
495	`greater_than` and `less_than` convert both sides to numbers, so `2` and `"2"` behave the same. Use them for counters.
496	
497	### Order of evaluation
498	
499	After each user message, routing runs in this order. The first match wins and routing stops.
500	
501	```text
502	1. loop_condition of the current node    match: stay in the node, use loop_prompt
503	2. the node's transitions, in list order match: go to target_node
504	3. global nodes                          match: enter the global node
505	4. nothing matched                       stay in the node, wait for the next user message
506	```
507	
508	Within step 2:
509	
510	- Transitions are checked in list order. Put specific conditions first and broad ones last.
511	- Deterministic conditions are evaluated first. If one matches, no routing model call is made.
512	- If several transitions of a node have the same `target_node`, the engine merges them at load time into one transition. Its condition is the OR of the originals. If one of them is unconditional, the merged transition is unconditional.
513	
514	Routing also runs after a tool result arrives. Verified in a working builder: a transition on a variable that a tool's `response_mapping` sets fires in the same turn, without a further user message.
515	
516	When nothing matches, there is no fallback. The agent stays and answers from the same `task_message`. Make sure every realistic path has a matching transition.
517	
518	### `routing_prompt`
519	
520	A node-level string. It replaces the default intent-matching instruction of the routing model for this node. Use it when the transition descriptions cannot carry the rule, for example "stay here until both the name and the date are given".
521	
522	### Self-transition
523	
524	A last transition with `always` that targets the node itself keeps the user in the node until an earlier transition matches.
525	
526	```json
527	{ "target_node": "collect_details", "description": "Keep collecting", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
528	```
529	
530	Prefer this to `loop_condition` in most cases. All routing then lives in one ordered list.
531	
532	### Loop conditions
533	
534	`loop_condition` is an intent description. The routing model checks it before all transitions. When it matches, the agent stays in the node.
535	
536	`loop_prompt` replaces `task_message` in the system message from the second turn in the node. The model sees one of the two, never both. Write it so that it stands alone. `{{var}}` works in it, so it can show what was already collected.
537	
538	```json
539	{
540	  "name": "collect_contact",
541	  "node_type": "conversation",
542	  "task_message": "Ask for the caller's full name and email address.",
543	  "loop_condition": "The user has not yet given both a full name and an email address",
544	  "loop_prompt": "Name so far: {{customer_name}}. Email so far: {{email}}. Ask only for what is still missing. When both are present, read them back once.",
545	  "transitions": []
546	}
547	```
548	
549	Make the loop condition specific. "The user has not finished" matches everything and the agent never leaves.
550	
551	### Tool-call transitions
552	
553	Set `is_tool_call` to `true` on a transition. The dialogue model then sees the transition as a tool named `transition_to_<node>` and triggers it by calling that tool. The router does not evaluate it after each turn.
554	
555	```json
556	{
557	  "target_node": "confirm_booking",
558	  "description": "The caller accepted the offered slot",
559	  "is_tool_call": true,
560	  "condition": { "operator": "matches_intent", "description": "The caller accepted the offered slot" }
561	}
562	```
563	
564	Use it when the agent should decide to move, for example because of something it just said or computed. The agent can acknowledge and move in the same message. The target node's `on_enter` then asks the next question. Global nodes accept the same flag.
565	
566	### Passthrough nodes
567	
568	A node with `"passthrough": true` routes right after its entry actions. It does not wait for the user. `api_request` and `code` nodes are normally passthrough nodes.
569	
570	- Set `passthrough_default_transition` to the next node.
571	- End `transitions` with an `always` transition. A passthrough node with no matching transition deadlocks.
572	- Set `on_enter` to `{"type": "silent"}`, or to a short fixed line that covers the wait.
573	
574	```json
575	{
576	  "name": "prepare",
577	  "node_type": "code",
578	  "passthrough": true,
579	  "passthrough_default_transition": "greeting",
580	  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
581	  "pre_actions": [],
582	  "transitions": [
583	    { "target_node": "greeting", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
584	  ]
585	}
586	```
587	
588	Verified in a working builder: a passthrough `code` node can be the `initial_node`. It runs before the agent says anything.
589	
590	### Global nodes
591	
592	A global node is an interrupt handler. It can fire from any node. It is checked only after the current node's own transitions found no match.
593	
594	A global node has the same fields as a normal node, plus:
595	
596	| Field | Meaning |
597	|---|---|
598	| `condition` | When the global node activates. Same format as a transition condition |
599	| `description` | Purpose of the node |
600	| `excluded_nodes` | Array of node keys where it must not fire |
601	| `is_tool_call` | Offer the global node to the dialogue model as a tool, not as a per-turn check |
602	
603	`__previous__` as a `target_node` or as `passthrough_default_transition` returns to the node that was interrupted.
604	
605	```json
606	{
607	  "global_nodes": {
608	    "off_topic": {
609	      "name": "off_topic",
610	      "description": "Brings the caller back to the subject",
611	      "condition": { "operator": "matches_intent", "description": "The user talks about something unrelated to their order" },
612	      "task_message": "Redirect the caller to the subject.",
613	      "on_enter": { "type": "tts", "text": "I can only help with your order. Let us continue." },
614	      "passthrough": true,
615	      "passthrough_default_transition": "__previous__",
616	      "excluded_nodes": ["goodbye"],
617	      "transitions": [
618	        { "target_node": "__previous__", "description": "always", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
619	      ]
620	    }
621	  }
622	}
623	```
624	
625	Rules:
626	
627	- List terminal nodes in `excluded_nodes`, or the global node can loop.
628	- Exclude nodes where an interrupt would do harm, for example an identity check.
629	- For a plain redirect use a passthrough node with a fixed line. It is faster and more predictable than a model reply.
630	- Use global nodes for interrupts that can happen anywhere. Do not copy the same transition into every node.
631	
632	## Extraction schema
633	
634	`extraction_schema` is an array on a node. After each user message the extraction model fills the listed variables from the conversation.
635	
636	```json
637	{
638	  "extraction_schema": [
639	    {
640	      "name": "order_number",
641	      "type": "string",
642	      "description": "The order number the caller reads out",
643	      "validation_pattern": "^[0-9]{8}$",
644	      "max_retries": 2,
645	      "min_confidence": 0.8
646	    },
647	    {
648	      "name": "request_type",
649	      "type": "string",
650	      "enum_values": ["status", "cancel", "change_address", "other"],
651	      "description": "What the caller wants to do with the order",
652	      "min_confidence": 0.7
653	    }
654	  ]
655	}
656	```
657	
658	| Field | Type | Meaning |
659	|---|---|---|
660	| `name` | string | Variable name |
661	| `type` | string | `string`, `integer`, `float`, `boolean`, `date`, `datetime`, `name`, `phone_number` |
662	| `description` | string | What the variable is |
663	| `enum_values` | array | Allowed values. Works on every type. The old `enum` type is deprecated and becomes `string` |
664	| `extraction_prompt` | string | A custom extraction template. See the warning below |
665	| `validation_pattern` | string | Regular expression the value must match |
666	| `min_confidence` | number | 0.0 to 1.0. Values below it are discarded. Default `0.95` |
667	| `max_retries` | integer | Retries after a failed validation, with the error given to the model |
668	
669	How it works:
670	
671	1. The extraction model sees recent messages and the schema.
672	2. It returns structured values.
673	3. Confidence is computed from the model's token probabilities, not from a self-report.
674	4. Each value is checked against `validation_pattern` and `enum_values`.
675	5. On failure the model retries, up to `max_retries`.
676	
677	Rules:
678	
679	- **Set `min_confidence` on every variable.** The default of 0.95 is strict. A discarded value leaves no trace in the transcript, so it looks the same as "nothing was extracted".
680	- **`extraction_prompt` replaces the whole built-in template.** It is not appended. A custom prompt must contain the input placeholders itself: `{{extractor.speech}}`, `{{extractor.conversation.last-10}}`, `{{extractor.type_preamble}}` and `{{extractor.variables_list}}`. Without them the extractor never sees the user's message and returns nothing on every turn, while dialogue and routing look healthy.
681	- **Declare dates as `type: "date"`.** The date types give the extractor today's date and the rules for relative dates such as "tomorrow". A date typed as `string` gets no date anchor and the model guesses the year.
682	- The built-in date rules turn vague expressions such as "next week" into a concrete date. If you need vague dates rejected, a custom prompt must say so and state that this overrides the general rules.
683	- No `null`. Omit optional fields or use `""`.
684	- An extracted variable is available to the same node's transitions in the same turn, and to every later node.
685	
686	Inside `extraction_prompt` these date placeholders resolve: `{{date.today}}`, `{{time.now}}`, `{{date.day_of_week}}`, `{{date.yesterday}}`, `{{date.tomorrow}}`, `{{date.day_after_tomorrow}}`, `{{date.next_week}}`, `{{date.end_of_month}}`, `{{date.first_next_month}}`, `{{date.next_mon}}` to `{{date.next_sun}}`, `{{date.last_mon}}` to `{{date.last_sun}}`, `{{date.fnm_mon}}` to `{{date.fnm_sun}}` (first such weekday of next month), `{{date.weeks2}}`, `{{date.weeks3}}`, `{{date.weeks2_ago}}`, `{{date.weeks3_ago}}`. Do not rely on them outside extraction prompts.
687	
688	**Fork on an extracted enum.** To route from one node to several paths, extract an enum and branch with `equals`. This is more reliable than several competing `matches_intent` transitions.
689	
690	```json
691	{
692	  "name": "menu",
693	  "node_type": "conversation",
694	  "task_message": "Tell the caller the order status in one sentence. Then ask whether they want to change the delivery address, cancel the order, or end the call.",
695	  "extraction_schema": [
696	    {
697	      "name": "next_action",
698	      "type": "string",
699	      "enum_values": ["change_address", "cancel", "done"],
700	      "description": "What the caller chose. Empty if unclear.",
701	      "min_confidence": 0.7
702	    }
703	  ],
704	  "transitions": [
705	    { "target_node": "change_address", "description": "Change address", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "next_action", "operator": "equals", "operand": "change_address" } ] } },
706	    { "target_node": "cancel_order", "description": "Cancel", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "next_action", "operator": "equals", "operand": "cancel" } ] } },
707	    { "target_node": "goodbye", "description": "Done", "condition": { "logic": "or", "conditions": [ { "variable": "next_action", "operator": "equals", "operand": "done" } ] } },
708	    { "target_node": "menu", "description": "Unclear, stay", "condition": { "operator": "always" } }
709	  ]
710	}
711	```
712	
713	Use extraction for user speech. For API responses use `response_mapping` (tools-and-code.md). It is deterministic and needs no model call.
714	
715	## End-call nodes
716	
717	An `end_call` node hangs up. It has a `terminal` object and no outgoing transitions.
718	
719	```json
720	{
721	  "name": "goodbye",
722	  "node_type": "end_call",
723	  "on_enter": { "type": "silent" },
724	  "disable_inactivity_monitor": true,
725	  "transitions": [],
726	  "terminal": {
727	    "type": "function",
728	    "function": {
729	      "name": "closing_end",
730	      "handler": "__function__:end_call",
731	      "parameters": {
732	        "type": "object",
733	        "properties": {
734	          "message_mode": { "type": "string", "default": "custom" },
735	          "spoken_message": { "type": "string", "default": "Thank you for calling. Goodbye." }
736	        }
737	      }
738	    }
739	  }
740	}
741	```
742	
743	| Parameter | Meaning |
744	|---|---|
745	| `message_mode` | `custom`: say `spoken_message`. `llm`: the model writes the farewell from `llm_prompt`. `none`: hang up without a farewell |
746	| `spoken_message` | The fixed farewell for `custom`. `{{var}}` works |
747	| `llm_prompt` | The instruction for `llm` |
748	| `interruptible` | `true` opens a short window after the farewell in which the user can still speak. Default: hang up as soon as the agent stops speaking |
749	| `trigger_timeout` | Length of that window in seconds |
750	| `trigger_pattern_both` | Farewell phrases, separated by `\|`, that do not cancel the close. Anything else the user says in the window cancels the close and returns the turn to the agent |
751	
752	Rules:
753	
754	- **The farewell comes from the terminal, not from `on_enter`.** A node with an `on_enter` line and `message_mode: "none"` hangs up silently. Put the sentence in `spoken_message` and set `on_enter` to `{"type": "silent"}`.
755	- Set `disable_inactivity_monitor` to `true` and `transitions` to `[]`.
756	- **The call's `endedReason` is the terminal's `function.name`.** The node name does not affect it. Pick a name that describes the outcome.
757	- Use several end-call nodes with different farewells and function names when outcomes differ.
758	- If you set `interruptible`, also set `trigger_pattern_both`. Without a phrase list every polite reply cancels the hang-up. The window is timed on a wall clock and a chat simulation cannot measure it.
759	
760	Verified in a working builder: `message_mode: "none"` with a silent `on_enter` ends the call when the node is reached. The agent says its goodbye in the previous conversation node.
761	
762	## Limits
763	
764	| Limit | Default | Notes |
765	|---|---|---|
766	| `max_node_turns` | `10` | Cap on user turns in one node. Only user messages count. Tool results and agent messages do not. There is no "unlimited" value |
767	| `max_turn_transition` | none | Where to go when the cap is reached. Without it the engine records the overrun and continues with normal routing, so the cap changes nothing |
768	| `truncation_strategy` | `keep_all` | `keep_all`: full history. `keep_recent`: system message plus the last `truncation_window_size` messages. `summarize`: older messages are replaced by a model-written summary |
769	| `truncation_window_size` | `10` | Used by `keep_recent` and `summarize` |
770	| Extraction `min_confidence` | `0.95` | See "Extraction schema" |
771	| Code `timeout_ms` | `30000` | See tools-and-code.md |
772	
773	Notes:
774	
775	- Truncation applies to the dialogue model only. Extraction and routing run before it.
776	- Give every node that sets `max_node_turns` a `max_turn_transition`. The working builder sets `max_node_turns` to 60 and 80 on its conversation nodes without a `max_turn_transition`. Its calls ended well below those counts, so the behaviour at the cap is not confirmed by it.
777	- Size the cap from real conversations. A node that handles a whole call can need dozens of user turns.
778	- The maximum call length in a simulation is set with `maxCallDurationSeconds` (api.md).
779	
780	## Design rules
781	
782	- Use `snake_case` node keys that describe the step.
783	- Keep dialogue in `task_message`, routing in `transitions`, data capture in `extraction_schema`.
784	- Every path must reach an `end_call` node.
785	- Put deterministic conditions before `matches_intent` conditions.
786	- Every passthrough node ends with an `always` transition.
787	- A transition back to an earlier node is supported.
788	- Split a step into its own node when it has strict rules of its own or forms a clear state. Keep related optional actions together in one conversation node with several tools.
789

956	What the example shows:
957	
958	| Node | Feature |
959	|---|---|
960	| `collect` | Fixed opening line, extraction with a `date` type, AND group, self-transition, turn cap with a target |
961	| `find_slots` | Passthrough `api_request` node, baked parameters, node-level `response_mapping`, failure counter, `always` fallback |

964	# Tools and code
965	
966	This page describes how a workflow calls HTTP APIs and runs Python. Read [workflow-format.md](workflow-format.md) first.
967	
968	Statements marked "verified in a working builder" come from a builder that created a 6-node workflow through the REST API. The workflow has code nodes, `api_call` tools, post-hooks and transitions on tool results. Its agent passed its practice cases. Statements marked "seen in a trial call" come from the event log of a simulation call made with that builder.
969	
970	## Tool function shape
971	
972	Every external action is a **tool function**. The shape is the same wherever you attach it.
973	
974	```json
975	{
976	  "type": "function",
977	  "config": { "timeoutMs": 10000, "maxRetries": 2 },
978	  "function": {
979	    "name": "lookup_order",
980	    "handler": "__function__:api_call",
981	    "description": "Look up one order. CALL it when the caller asks about a specific order.",
982	    "parameters": {
983	      "type": "object",
984	      "properties": {
985	        "url": { "type": "string", "default": "https://api.example.com/v1/orders/lookup" },
986	        "method": { "type": "string", "default": "POST" },
987	        "headers": {
988	          "type": "object",
989	          "properties": { "Content-Type": { "type": "string", "default": "application/json" } }
990	        },
991	        "body": {
992	          "type": "object",
993	          "properties": {
994	            "customer_id": { "type": "string", "default": "{{customer_id}}" },
995	            "order_number": { "type": "string", "description": "Order number, digits only", "default": "{{order_number}}" }
996	          },
997	          "required": ["order_number"]
998	        }
999	      }
1000	    }
1001	  },
1002	  "response_mapping": [
1003	    { "path": "data.status", "variable": "order_status" }
1004	  ]
1005	}
1006	```
1007	
1008	| Field | Meaning |
1009	|---|---|
1010	| `type` | Always `"function"` |
1011	| `function.name` | Tool name. The model calls it by this name. Result variables are named after it |
1012	| `function.handler` | Which runtime executes the tool. See the table below |
1013	| `function.description` | Read by the dialogue model when the tool is in `tools`. Ignored in `pre_actions` |
1014	| `function.parameters` | JSON-schema object. `properties` holds the parameters |
1015	| `config.timeoutMs` | Timeout of one attempt, in milliseconds |
1016	| `config.maxRetries` | Tool-level retries of a failed call |
1017	| `config.interruptible` | `false` makes the tool run in the background. See "Background tools" |
1018	| `config.alwaysRunsAt` | Makes the tool a lifecycle tool. See "Lifecycle tools" |
1019	| `response_mapping` | Tool level, for tools in `tools`. Maps the result to variables |
1020	| `pre_process_code` | Python hook that runs before the call |
1021	| `post_process_code` | Python hook that runs after the call |
1022	
1023	| Handler | Runs |
1024	|---|---|
1025	| `__function__:api_call` | An HTTP request |
1026	| `__function__:code_exec` | A Python snippet in a sandbox |
1027	| `__function__:end_call` | Hangs up. Used in the `terminal` of an `end_call` node |
1028	
1029	Handlers for integrations, knowledge search, call transfer and rescheduling also exist. They are not needed here.
1030	
1031	`api_call` parameters:
1032	
1033	| Parameter | Meaning |
1034	|---|---|
1035	| `url` | Request URL. `{{var}}` works |
1036	| `method` | HTTP method |
1037	| `headers` | Object. Each header is a property with a `default` |
1038	| `body` | Object. Each body field is a property under `body.properties` |
1039	| `connect_retries` | Transport retries. See "Retries and timeouts" |
1040	
1041	## How a parameter gets its value
1042	
1043	One key decides, per parameter: `default`.
1044	
1045	| Declaration | Who supplies the value | Does the model see the parameter |
1046	|---|---|---|
1047	| `default` with a literal, or with a `{{var}}` that has a value | The workflow. The value is **baked** | No |
1048	| `default` with a `{{var}}` that has no value when the node is entered | The model | Yes, named after the variable, with the property's `type`, `description` and `enum` |
1049	| no `default` | The model | Yes |
1050	| `const` | Nobody. `const` does **not** bake | It only constrains the model's own output |
1051	
1052	Rules:
1053	
1054	- **Use `default` for fixed backend config** such as `url`, `method` and auth headers. At registration the engine moves every `default` into the tool's base config, resolves `{{var}}` from the variable table, and removes the field from the schema the model sees.
1055	- **Never use `const` for a value you want sent.** The engine reads only `default`. A `{{var}}` inside a `const` never resolves. An `api_call` whose `url` is a `const` fails with "URL is required".
1056	- **Baking happens when the node is entered.** A `{{var}}` default is resolved against the variable table at that moment.
1057	
1058	The working builder uses this for every tool: `customer_id` has `"default": "{{customer_id}}"` and is baked from a call variable. Every other body field has `"default": "{{<field name>}}"`, where no variable of that name exists, so the model fills it. Verified in a working builder.
1059	
1060	Seen in a trial call: the model's arguments are stored as `<tool>_args.<field>` in the variable table, for example `lookup_order_args.order_number`. They were not stored under the bare field name.
1061	
1062	Take care that a model-filled field does not share its name with a variable that is already set when the node is entered. The value would be baked and the model would never see the parameter.
1063	
1064	### `api_call` body field rules
1065	
1066	- Declare each body field as a leaf under `body.properties.<field>`.
1067	- Put the field's `type`, `description` and `enum` on that leaf. Put required fields in `body.required`.
1068	- Give each leaf its own `default`.
1069	- Do not put a field spec at the top level of `parameters.properties` next to a `body.default` template object. The engine looks for the spec at `body.properties.<field>`, does not find it, and the model sees only "Template variable: name". The `enum` and `description` are lost while the call still works.
1070	- A body that exists only as one `body.default` object also shows as an empty form in the dashboard editor. Saving from there removes the tool.
1071	
1072	A `code_exec` tool is different: its parameters are true top-level arguments. Declare a model-filled one as a top-level property without `default`.
1073	
1074	### When a baked variable has no value
1075	
1076	| Field type | Variable unset | Variable is `""` |
1077	|---|---|---|
1078	| Normal field in an engine-run call (`pre_actions`, lifecycle tool) | The field is dropped from the request. No error | The field is sent empty |
1079	| `code` of `code_exec` | The literal text `{{var}}` stays in the Python source and the snippet crashes | |
1080	
1081	Fix: make sure an earlier node always sets the variable, even to a sentinel value. In code, read variables from `vars` and do not splice them in with `{{var}}`.
1082	
1083	### Constrain model-filled parameters
1084	
1085	When a value must be one of a known set, do not use a free string. The model sometimes invents a value that looks plausible.
1086	
1087	- Use an `enum` on the leaf, and list the values in the `description` as well.
1088	- Or use a `number` that is an index into a list, with the valid range in the description. A pre-hook or the backend turns the index into the real value.
1089	- If neither is possible, name the exact source in the description and tell the model to copy the value unchanged.
1090	
1091	```json
1092	{
1093	  "type": "object",
1094	  "properties": {
1095	    "queue": {
1096	      "type": "string",
1097	      "description": "Team that takes over. One of: billing, delivery, returns.",
1098	      "enum": ["billing", "delivery", "returns"],
1099	      "default": "{{queue}}"
1100	    }
1101	  },
1102	  "required": ["queue"]
1103	}
1104	```
1105	
1106	## `pre_actions` versus `tools`
1107	
1108	The placement decides who fires the call.
1109	
1110	| Placement | Node type | Who calls it | When |
1111	|---|---|---|---|
1112	| `pre_actions` | `api_request`, `code` | The engine | On node entry, before any model turn |
1113	| `tools` | `conversation` | The dialogue model | During a turn, when the model decides to |
1114	| Workflow-level `tools` with `config.alwaysRunsAt` | none | The engine | At call start or call end |
1115	
1116	The platform removes `tools` from non-conversation nodes and `pre_actions` from conversation nodes. It does so without an error: the JSON you sent looks fine, the create call succeeds, and the stored node has an empty array. A node cannot use both.
1117	
1118	**Use `pre_actions`** when the call must always run and the model has nothing to decide. Example: after the order number is known, always fetch the order.
1119	
1120	**Use `tools`** when the call depends on what the user says. Example: cancel the order only if the caller asks for it.
1121	
1122	Differences in behaviour:
